terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase. In Latin corium is a person’s skin “only in comic or contemptuous sense” (Lewis & Short); this phrase is not in Lewis & Short or the loci collections.

terms.gloss: play with one’s own skin: risk one’s own hide
evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. corium: corio suo ludere, “at one’s own” risk; de alieno corio ludere, at another’s expense (Apul. M. 7)
Cic. Tull. 54 (Lewis & Short), s.v. corium: “to flog”
Traupman 100: corium alicūjus petere, be after someone’s hide
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives it as “to flog”; Traupman uses it for “be after someone’s hide”.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 100, checked against the searchable text and the page image (12 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
